https://www.dw.com/en/tupac-shakur-murde.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IzIb Duane "Keffe D" Davis is charged in Clark County, Nevada, with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon Image: Steve Marcus/REUTERS Advertisement The murder trial over Tupac Shakur's 1996 killing opened with prosecutors arguing that Duane "Keffe D" Davis planned the shooting . Almost three decades after the drive-by shooting they opened their case by telling jurors the rapper was shot dead in an act of gang revenge masterminded by a mobster. “Let’s be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew,” Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal said. Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is charged in Clark County, Nevada, with a single count of murder using a deadly weapon. The 63-year-old has pleaded not guilty. What the prosecution said about 'shot caller' Davis Davis ordered the killing after his nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson, had been beaten by a rival gang, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told a court in Las Vegas Tuesday. Palal showed videos Tuesday of Shakur's entourage attacking Anderson. "Then, two and a half hours later... Tupac is gunned down in a drive-by shooting from a white Cadillac in an act of revenge," the prosecutor told jurors. Palal said that Davis — who has been dubbed by the authorities as a "shot caller" — did not pull the trigger but "he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew". Palal went on to tell the jury: "Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself," referring to Davis' previous interviews with law enforcement and the media, as well as his autobiography, where the accused describes Shakur's killing. Davis said in the interviews and his 2019 memoir, "Compton Street Legend," that he was riding in the car from which Shakur was shot. In an interview with a federal task force probing another killing, Davis spoke of the Shakur shooting. He described handing a gun to the men in the backseat of the white Cadillac that fired on the rapper's black BMW. On Tuesday, prosecutors played audio of Davis explaining the moment Shakur was shot. Davis' defense rails against 'sloppy' investigation Representing Davis, attorney Michael Sanft called the prosecution's narrative "fiction" during the defense's opening statement. Sanft said prosecutors had no real proof that his client was culpable. He said that after 30 years a police investigation has repeatedly failed to turn up a definitive version of events. He called the investigation "biased," "sloppy" and "incomplete." "Just look at ‌the actual facts. What facts do you have to support any of what Keffe D said in any of his interviews or the book?" Sanft told the jury. The defense had fought to keep Davis' book out of the trial. Image: Steve Marcus/REUTERS Sanft further said the accounts he gave in interviews and his memoir ccould not be corroborated. Davis was seen at the trial wearing a blue suit and tie. He was also seen scanning the public gallery during testimony. As per Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder if he took part in the crime without firing the gun himself. If convicted, he faces the possibility of life imprisonment without parole. Meanwhile, the trial is expected to last up to six weeks. Tupac Shakur — a cultural icon Shakur, also known as 2Pac, was 25 when he was wounded in a drive-by shooting on Sept. 7, 1996. He succumbed to his injuries in hospital six days later. Shakur, who also went by the stage names 2Pac and Makaveli, is considered one of the most influential rappers of all time Image: Death Row Records/dpa/AFP/picture alliance Although his death cut his immensely popular music career short, Shakur remains one of the most influential and versatile rappers of all time. Shakur's music often addressed issues facing Black Americans. He was also a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast. Edited by: Louis Oelofse . https://www.torahmusings.com/2026/08/dre.text: by R. Gil Student Dreams are a common part of daily life to which the Talmudic Sages attribute great importance. They see in dreams both danger and opportunity, and therefore created three ceremonies or opportunities to rid ourselves of bad omens in dreams. However, on a more careful look, we find conflicting thoughts about dreams in the Talmud and a steadily decreasing concern for them over the ages. As the centuries passed, life changed dramatically and dreams seemed to lose some of their importance. Does that affect halakhah ? I. Responding to Dreams The Gemara ( Shabbos 11a) says that fasting is effective to neutralize a bad dream like a fire burns kindling. If you have a bad dream, you may fast even on Shabbos, a day on which fasting is normally forbidden. Another option is mentioned in a different Gemara ( Berakhos 55b). If you have a bad dream that bothers you, you should gather three friends and have them interpret it positively, i.e. tell you that it is really a good dream. This will eliminate the negative impact of the dream. A further practice is to recite a standard formula during the priestly blessings ( Birkas Kohanim ) asking for positive outcomes from your dreams. This all implies a serious concern for dreams. Similarly, the Gemara ( Nedarim 8a) says that if you are excommunicated in a dream, you should gather ten men to undo the excommunication. The commentators (Ran and Rosh, ad loc.) say that even though this occurred only in a dream, we are concerned that you were excommunicated in Heaven. And yet, another passage indicates a different attitude. The Gemara ( Sanhedrin 30a) says that if your father comes to you in a dream and says that certain money he left for you is forbidden for specific reasons, you can ignore the dream because “Matters in a dream have neither positive nor negative impact ( divrei chalomos lo ma’alin ve-lo yordin ).” We do not rely on dreams for practical matters; therefore you can safely ignore them. In a different instance, a legal guardian for orphans was selling their land for a reckless investment, to which R. Meir objected ( Gittin 52a). R. Meir saw in a dream that this reckless sale was desired by Heaven but he continued in his opposition because, “Matters in a dream have neither positive nor negative impact.” But if dreams have no practical impact, why do we have different options for trying to neutralize them including fasting on Shabbos? II. Are Dreams Important? Rav Shimon Ben Tzemach Duran (Rashbatz, 15th cen., Algeria; Responsa Tashbetz 2:128 ) suggests that the case in Sanhedrin involves someone else dreaming about your father saying that the money is forbidden. We do not believe someone else’s dreams about you. However, we believe a dream that you have about yourself. While that might explain the passage in Sanhedrin , in Gittin R. Meir dreamed about himself and still ignored his dream. Rather, he quotes Rava ( Berakhos 55b) who contrasts two verses. On the one hand, God says “I speak with him in a dream” (Num. 12:6), implying that there is divine truth in a dream. On the other hand, “the dreams speak falsely” (Zech. 10:12). Rava answers that dreams transmitted by angels are true but those transmitted by demons are not. According to Rashbatz, the angel here means divine providence and the demon means an unhealthy imagination for any of a number of reasons. In other words, some dreams are true — messages from Heaven — and some are false, caused by psychological forces, physiological phenomena or otherwise. Therefore, we are left in doubt whether any specific dream is true. We do not divest someone of money for a doubtful claim; therefore dreams have no impact on monetary matters. However, when something is forbidden and easily remedied, we put in the effort to make it permissible when there is even a doubt. Therefore, you should undo an excommunication that occurs in a dream or fast to neutralize dream. In Medieval times, we start to find authorities questioning whether people still have bad dreams that emerge from a divine source. The Tur (15th cen., Germany/Spain; Orach Chaim 568) quotes R. Amram, R. Kalonymus and R. Eliezer Ben Yoel (Ra’aviah) who say that today (in their day), we do not know which dreams are truly bad and therefore you should not fast on Shabbos over a dream. Rav Yosef Karo (16th cen., Israel; Beis Yosef , ad loc.) quotes other Medieval authorities with similar hesitations but Rav Karo ( Shulchan Arukh , ad loc., 5; 288:4-5) does not follow those authorities completely, and allows fasting on Shabbos for dreams listed in the Talmud. We find additional concerns in later generations. III. Should We Worry About Dreams? Rav Avraham Gombiner (17th cen., Poland; Magen Avraham 288:7) quotes approvingly Rav Yeshayahu Horowitz (17th cen., Germany; Shenei Luchos Ha-Beris, Shabbos , s.v. ve-sa’anis chalom ) who says that you should not fast on Shabbos for any dream. Rav Ovadiah Yosef (21st cen., Israel; Yechaveh Da’as 4:24) quotes Rav Horowitz as going even further (I could not find this passage). Rav Horowitz quotes the Gemara ( Pesachim 110b) about a demonic problem of doing things in even numbers (such as drinking 2 or 4 cups). The Gemara says that someone who is concerned about this will be taken to task for doing it; someone who is not concerned for this will not face negative repercussions. If you are worried about doing things in even numbers, then if for some reason you drink 2 cups (rather than 1 or 3), then the demons will make trouble for you. If you don’t care, then it doesn’t matter if you drink 2 cups. Rav Horowitz says the same applies to bad dreams — if they worry you, then you need to be concerned and possibly fast over them. If you aren’t worried about a bad dream, then you have no reason for concern. [1] See also Responsa Rivash, no. 513. But can you control whether you are scared by a bad dream? We can assume that bad dreams are not from a divine source. Therefore, Rav Ovadiah Yosef (ibid.) concludes by quoting Rav Chaim Palaggi (19th cen., Turkey; Ruach Chaim 288:1) that if you have a bad dream on Shabbos, rather than fasting you should say extra Tehillim and study Torah diligently. Elsewhere, Rav Yosef seems unconcerned with bad dreams, almost as if they are a practical joke on you that you should ignore ( Beis Ha-Yayin , Yamim Nora’im , pp. 195-196). You should just say the verse “the dreams speak falsely” or, if you are very worried, take the standard formula ( Ribbono Shel Olam ) that is used for Birkas Kohanim , and say it on your own on any day, even without Birkas Kohanim . And, if you are very worried and you are greatly pained, then you may follow the Gemara and fast on Shabbos (fulfilling all the halakhic details). Going even further, Rav Avraham Yeshayahu Karelitz (Chazon Ish, 20th cen., Israel; Kovetz Iggeros Chazon Ish , vol. 2, no. 149 ) writes briefly that personally he just ignores his bad dreams. He continues that if you have a bad dream, say the Ribbono Shel Olam and move on with your day. We cannot just tell someone not to worry about their dream but we can redirect them to a brief verse or prayer. Rav Simcha Rabinowitz (cont., Israel; Piskei Teshuvos 220:1) explains Chazon Ish’s approach. In modern times, people are busier and their lives are more filled with global concerns than in ancient times. Nowadays, dreams are about what we hear during our busy days and the concerns we face in our lives. Therefore, we should not pay much attention to our dreams because they are not divine predictions about the future. Rather, they are manifestations of our thoughts, which might give insight into our psychological well-being but will not tell us what will happen in the future. The Chazon Ish died in 1953. At that time, there were daily newspapers and radio programs so that modern media was spreading news quickly. I am old enough to remember when, if you wanted to get the latest news, you had to watch the news at certain times or listen to the radio every twenty two minutes. And if you wanted to check stock prices, you had to read the morning newspaper. Then came 24-hour news channels and financial news. Then came the internet, with breaking news and real-time financial information. Now we have social media, with constant updates and opinions. The pace of life today is much faster than it was forty years ago, and even more so than it was four hundred years ago. Modern communication brings us so much news and information that overwhelm our dreams. If you are worried that your dreams might come true, you can recite the specific verses or formulas about dreams. However, according to Chazon Ish and others, there is no need to do so. (reposted from May ’22) Endnotes [ + ] Endnotes ↑ 1 See also Responsa Rivash, no. 513. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/nicusor-.text: Nicușor Dan on Ukraine’s Independence Day: Romania will continue to stand with Kyiv Romania will continue to support Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, Nicușor Dan said in a message posted on X and addressed, among others, to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The message comes as Ukraine marks its Independence Day on August 24, 35 years after declaring independence from the Soviet Union. Nicușor Dan: Romania will continue to stand with Ukraine The Romanian president congratulated the Ukrainian authorities and people and referred to their resistance in the face of the war launched by Russia. “On the occasion of Ukraine’s Independence Day, Romania extends its warmest congratulations, together with wishes for peace, security and prosperity. Today, we honor the extraordinary courage and heroic resilience of the Ukrainian people in defending our shared values and freedom,” Nicușor Dan wrote. The head of state stressed that Bucharest would continue its support at a time when developments in the war in neighboring Ukraine also have direct implications for Romania’s security and for NATO’s entire eastern flank. “Romania will continue to stand with Ukraine, firmly supporting the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity. Ukraine can count on our multidimensional assistance,” the president said. Bucharest supports Ukraine’s EU accession and reconstruction Nicușor Dan also referred to the period following the end of the conflict, reaffirming Romania’s commitment to Ukraine’s European integration and post-war reconstruction. “Romania also remains fully committed to supporting Ukraine’s EU accession process and its post-conflict reconstruction,” the head of state said. For Romania, Ukraine’s accession to the European Union is of particular importance, as the two countries share a border of more than 600 kilometers. Bucharest is also among the supporters of EU enlargement toward countries in the Union’s eastern neighborhood. Nicușor Dan highlights NATO’s importance for regional security The Romanian president also addressed the security dimension, arguing that NATO’s continued engagement with Ukraine remains essential. “At the same time, NATO’s continued engagement alongside Ukraine remains essential for the long-term stability and security of the entire Euro-Atlantic area,” Nicușor Dan said. https://www.e-flux.com/notes/6783544/loc.text: Thank you for your interest in e-flux . Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. September 3, 2026 Locarno International Film Festival 79 George MacBeth Ana Vaz, Hanabi , 2026. Courtesy of Tambores a noite / Les Volcans. In a performance from 1968, Hollis Frampton projected a stark rectangle of white light onto a wall. The “film” in question was the Fluxus artist Takehisa Kosugi’s work Film/Film#4 (1965). Through a tape recorder, Michael Snow narrated Frampton’s impressions of Kosugi’s seemingly radical act of reduction: It is only a rectangle of white light. But it is all films. We can never see more within our rectangle, only less … But aside from that, we must agree that this [film] is, from an aesthetic point of view, incomparably superior to a large proportion of films that have ever been made. But we have decided that we want to see less than this. Very well. 1 A pure white light contains within it the entire visible spectrum of color. Yet Frampton’s point was not simply tautological. I thought of this episode as I sat near the summit of Cardada-Cimetta, 1400 feet above the Lago Maggiore, surrounded by pinky-indigo Alpine peaks, to stare like millions of others in Europe at the eclipse. The crowd of locals gathering in the Piazza Grande far below, the hobnobbing in the Campari bars, the agitated post-screening discussions of films most of us would likely forget as soon as the festival subsided, seemed now all very far away. Through the twin rectangles of my eclipse glasses, the spectrum of ultraviolet, visible, and infrared rays was radically diminished until all that remained in my field of vision was the molten globule of the sun getting gradually gnawed away by the moon. I watched it transfigure from an open-mouthed Pacman to a clementine slice, to a perfect croissant, until all that was left was a crisp orange cuticle hung in the middle distance. Soon a cloud drifted across, I took off my specs, and the world returned. Perhaps it’s a touch unfair to set the “incomparably superior” aesthetic experience of the Alpine solar eclipse, an event that last happened in Switzerland twenty-six years ago, against the films presented at the 79th Locarno International Film Festival—which annually brings cinephiles to the slightly hyperreal splendor of this lakeside resort town. That the eclipse did prove the most visionary and enduring thing I beheld during my time in Ticino was just inauspicious timing, I suppose. “We have decided that we want to see less than this. Very well.” Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence , 2026. Courtesy of Heretic Films. A major debutantes’ ball on the circuit for independent and art house films, Locarno historically treads a path between the demands of the tourism industries, which in part financially sustain it, and “pure” cinephilia. The nightly screenings in the vast Piazza Grande (where this year one could watch Nicolas Cage high-kicking his way through Wild at Heart and Eddie Murphy’s The Nutty Professor ) cater to the former camp, while the retrospectives and shorts programming service the latter. Recent years have also seen notable overtures from the festival towards experimental artist filmmakers. In 2023 the art collector and LUMA Foundation president Maja Hoffman was appointed president. The festival’s director Giona A. Nazzaro also recently scrapped the “Moving Ahead” sidebar program dedicated to experimental film, with the rationale of allowing more avant-garde, nonnarrative work to commingle into a richer, more pluralistic program. Halfway through my stay in Locarno, I found myself at a panel titled “A World Without Film Critics,” prompted no doubt by the juvenile dream of attending your own funeral. The room was jam-packed (with film critics, naturally). The discussion went beyond mere professional status anxiety: Was the crisis of criticism parasitic upon the crisis of cinema itself? Were we also facing the gradual extinction of the nonprofessional cineaste? Why is it that only multimillion-dollar blockbusters like the Odyssey —rather than the art house productions on show at festivals like Locarno—seem able to seriously kick the hornet’s nest of critical discourse in 2026? And how can film writers effectively torque their language to outmaneuver AI and better capture what Raymond Bellour called that “fundamentally elusive object” of film? Do we just, as Diego Cepeda (editor of Outskirts magazine) suggested, all need to return to reading Joyce? The Golden Leopard (Locarno’s top prize) this year went to Romanian New Wave director Florin Șerban’s You Don’t Belong Here , a well-scripted moral fable about anti-Roma racism regrettably shot and color-graded with the hyperbolic sobriety of a 2000s-era anti-drugs infomercial. A more deserving recipient would have been Denis Côté’s Nobody’s Violence . A goth-punk reckoning with the febrile discussion in Canada around MAID (medical assistance in dying), Côté’s film follows a terse and spectral black-market euthanist called Mira (a superb turn from Larissa Corriveau) working the beat of a small town in Quebec. Mira says little, lives in her van with her Jack Russell, and seems at first temperamentally well equipped for her grim occupation. Though the film initially appears as a homage to Claude Chabrol’s Story of Women (1988), Côté soon warps and wends his narrative in unexpected directions that force Mira to interrogate her own attachments to the world. Made, as ever for Côté, on a shoestring budget, and lensed in a bristly mix of vintage and expired 16 mm stock, the director wrote the script while himself suffering from a kidney disease that left him unsure if he would live or die, pending a donor. These heightened existential stakes are apparent as the film spurs itself into almost convulsive outbursts of spirit and liveliness, particularly during two brilliant extended sequences. First there is Mira’s meet-cute with a faintly deranged party-boy called Flanagan, and next a raucous dinner party at the house of her lecherous handler Ludo, both of which explode the grimness of her routines. There is an antic, restless inventiveness to Côté’s whip-cuts and compositions, which renders his choice to film in a wraithlike 16 mm totally apposite, imbuing his images with gothic dread. This medium-sensitivity was not so evident in several of the other 16 mm films I saw at the festival (a rough tally put my count at fifteen, though surely there were more), which more often than not seemed to have alighted on the decision to shoot on an “artisanal” stock through nothing more impassioned than professional osmosis. When artist filmmakers first began returning to “obsolescent” formats en masse around the turn of the millennium, light-leaky images bearing the traces of their own materiality were consciously favored over the more current options of digital or video. Often these media were conceived as a means for meditating on the “nostalgia for the ruined dreams of twentieth-century modernity,” as Erika Balsom once wrote of Tacita Dean’s work. Yet the once programmatic engagement with analogue and expired film formats appears to have ossified in the moving image community into something largely irreflective or automatic, to the point where at festivals like Locarno such images increasingly feel like a ready-to-hand imprimatur of suitability for the festival circuit: a warm, one-size-fits-all visual strategy for immediately siloing films off to the “survival compound” of the white cube. Ann Oren, Objet A , 2026. Courtesy of Schuldenberg Films. One of this year’s more anticipated titles was the second feature from Ann Oren, Objet A (the Lacan nod is intentional). The film follows Ingeborg and Adam, an haute-bourgeois couple working as hand surgeons who live in an upscale Berlin apartment. In her press conference Oren spoke of her desire in Objet A to explore haptics, tactility, and the larger erotics of touch we have lost through continuously swiping, pinching, and pawing at our LCD screens. She sets the stage for this early on in the film with rhythmic cuts that delight in the thwack of Adam’s newspaper at the breakfast table, the swish of satin sheets in their bedroom, the whirr of a polaroid camera, the slice of vintage fan blades, the ignition of their vintage Saab. They don’t have phones. There is a particularly telling scene in which Ingeborg scowls disapprovingly at people watching Instagram reels around her on the U-Bahn (might we catch the director scowling along with her?). After Ingeborg fractures her leg, a former patient of the couple’s, Gaia, is drawn into their life as their assistant. To borrow from the argot of polyamory, Gaia rapidly becomes their “unicorn,” a source of anguish and erotic fascination. Gaia—who wears an organic hessian dress and speaks in riddles—embodies a closeness to and kinship with the natural world that is absent from Adam and Ingeborg’s monomaniac lives. Her deepening involvement with the pair soon prompts spores of fungi to sprout in their minimalist home, a forest to encircle it, and a genuinely lysergic closing sequence in which the trio together approach a prelapsarian bliss in the forest. In its modish and unconvincing effort at presenting adjustments to one’s lifestyle as a form of eco-critique, Objet A felt symptomatic of the limited horizons of romantic anti-capitalism. This compost heap of art house cliches made me wistful for an era when art house filmmakers dared confront the psychic and comic affordances of the transfiguring socio-technical apparatus, rather than simply expressing a sophisticate’s horror at their vulgarity. By the time the credits rolled, Oren’s retromania had begun to remind me of the once-common sight in Stoke Newington of a barista riding a penny farthing with a handlebar moustache. Elham Ehsas, Forgotten Spaceman , 2026. Courtesy of MonoFilm Productions. Locarno’s program this year was also replete with disembodied and disjointed voices, murmuring in and out of sync with the images on screen, or wandering off on parallel narrative circuits altogether. These distant narrators can be understood as what sound and film theorist Michel Chion has termed acousmêtre— the voices we hear but never see, like a call center phone operator, or the voice of our mother while we’re still inside the womb. For Chion, the acousmêtre is a source of “disequilibrium and tension,” something partially outside of the film but nevertheless guiding it from within, which possesses dark powers of ubiquity, panopticism, omniscience, and omnipotence. 2 In Forgotten Spaceman , Elham Ehsas’s fascinating video-essay on Abdul Ahad Momand, the first (and only) Afghan sent into orbit, the filmmaker’s disembodied voice-over is enunciative—as he wistfully strikes up a one-way correspondence with the forgotten spaceman, accompanied by his own father’s highly saturated archival footage of the space mission (which the director found in the digitized archive of Afghan Films rescued by the CAMP collective). “From space we don’t see the borders we die for.” Much like Joana Hadjithomas and Khalil Joreige’s The Lebanese Rocket Society , Ehsas’s film is an exercise in counter-memory, which reactivates a moment of cosmic optimism to illuminate, in his words, “how nations forget and how their exiled children remember.” The pathos of combining this enunciative mode of address with archival footage was also pursued, albeit less successfully, in Mohanad Yaqubi’s Revolutionaries Never Die , a film which again strikes up an intimate correspondence between the filmmaker and his subject: the Lebanese documentarian Jocelyne Saab. While Yaqubi’s work in restoring Saab’s exhilarating documentaries on various militant, anti-imperialist struggles across the Arab world from 1973–83 has been of immeasurable benefit, his obtrusive commentary over her footage in Revolutionaries Never Die (“Jocelyn, the closer I grow to your process the more I regret not replying to your email sooner”) ultimately left one wishing that the festival had chosen to program a retrospective of Saab’s newly restored films instead. One of the more peculiar films playing in the competition, Nicolaas Schmidt’s wordless September Afternoon , also used its audio track to notable effect. While his images tell a modest story of a young couple taking their child on a trip to a windy beach along the Nordsee, and dwell in a somewhat familiar slow-cinema mode on the depiction of them methodically packing up and erecting the tent, Schmidt chooses to accompany these long shots with a hypnotic loop of the bridge to Billy Idol’s “Eyes Without a Face,” mixed alongside diegetic audio of the beach’s roaring wind and tide. When it works, as during a ten-minute sequence of the silent protagonist walking along the shoreline, this looping sonic mélange of eighties pop and ocean gale was oddly captivating—capturing the faint dread of an earworm that entangles itself into your thoughts against your will. Meanwhile in Ana Vaz’s second feature, Hanabi , the Brazilian video artist also works along the seam between sound and image. Vaz freely adapts the Japanese writer Yoko Hayasuke’s Journal of a Radioactive Brain —a diaristic essay he wrote in the wake of the tsunami and the Fukushima nuclear disaster that followed the Tohoku earthquake—into a script to accompany her sumptuous Bolex footage of the post-disaster everyday (following evacuees, nuclear scientists turned beekeepers, and business as usual). By mixing her own deadpan voice-over, Hayasuke’s mordant reflections, and the steady tick of Geiger counters on the soundtrack, Vaz invests footage of seemingly placid urban tableaux with the ambient threat of a radioactive brain: When everything could be radioactive, how do we know this isn’t? As in Defoe’s Journal of a Plague Year , the fear of contagion restructures the experience of the quotidian in Hanabi , despite how oddly calm everything looks and seems. There are few certainties in 2026. This summer will probably have been the hottest on record, the next election results will be disappointing for the left, and Hong Sang Soo will release on average two films a year until either you or he dies. His latest, Nowhere to Lay My Eyes , was an affecting, if oddly withholding, tale of two siblings on a trip to Jeju Island to visit their estranged mother, which carried many of what have become the hallmarks of his style. These include soft, Morandi-ish compositions (which since In Water [2023] have been ever so slightly out-of-focus), long, uninterrupted takes of naturalistic conversations in which a crash zoom suddenly occurs, lo-fi music, and an aversion to close-ups and montage. Yet the style of Hong’s approach to filmmaking lies increasingly in how this set of hallmark visual and narratological strategies have been intercombined, adapted, and accumulated over the years, so that, like Tancredi declares in Leopardi’s The Leopard , in a Hong Sang-Soo film, “for things to stay the same, everything has to change.” He never uses the same device in the same way twice. This latest film is no exception. What especially jumped out to me here was his reprisal of the voice-over, which he hasn’t used since Grass (2018). As in that film, the voice in question is Kim Min-Hee’s. Her occasional voice-over track becomes a means for Min-hee’s character Sanghee, herself an experimental filmmaker, to express her inner lyricism, and the discomfiture she feels during an agonized, stilted weekend spent with a mother who seems like a stranger to her. So far, so straightforward; the voice-over as backdoor into subjectivity. Yet the torque Hong applies is to mix the diegetic noise of the scene and that of Min-hee’s voice at exactly the same level, rather than for the latter to submerge the former. It’s a deceptively simple trick whose effect is arresting—one of those softly Brechtian maneuvers that proves what Dennis Lim calls the “countervailing tendencies” throughout Hong’s work, that “even as hi

Photograph: CPS/PA Greater Manchester Man who ran over cyclist and dragged him under car for a mile convicted of murder Simon Richardson knew headteacher Michael Mullins was under his 4×4 as he kept driving in Manchester, jury heard Mark Brown North of England correspondent Fri 30 Oct 2026 11.05 EDT First published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 08.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A motorist who drove through give-way markings, collided with a cyclist and then dragged him, trapped under his car, for more than a mile has been found guilty of murder. Simon Richardson, 35, crashed into headteacher Michael Mullins, 56, who was cycling home from work at Stretford grammar school, Greater Manchester, on the evening of 20 April. Mullins hit the bonnet and windscreen of Richardson’s Volvo XC90 and then went under the car, becoming entangled in the suspension. Richardson continued to drive for more than a mile, knowing that the trapped cyclist was just inches under his feet, a trial at Manchester Minshull Street crown court heard. View image in fullscreen Family photograph of Michael Mullins. Photograph: Greater Manchester police/PA Members of Mullins’ family were in tears after the guilty verdict was delivered on Friday. The trial judge, Mrs Justice Brunner KC, discharged jurors from taking jury service again for 10 years and told them: “This was, I know, an upsetting case and there was evidence which you may have found distressing.” Richardson had denied knowing the father-of-two was under his car but the prosecutor Phil Barnes KC said the defendant knew “and he inevitably knew what the consequences of driving on would be, and he did it anyway”. “For a split second after the collision, for a brief moment, he possibly thought about doing the right thing and getting out and taking ownership of what he had just done and help the man he had just run down. “But Simon Richardson did not get out. He did not do the right thing. He chose to drive away. The obvious reason is because he wanted to escape the consequences of what he had just done.” Richardson’s front-seat passenger, his cousin Gabrielle Debotte, told the trial they both heard “moaning” from outside as he drove away from the collision scene. Giving evidence for the prosecution, she said Richardson went on to say: “He’s under the car.” The collision happened in the village of Warburton. The court heard Richardson drove to a secluded farm track in Lymm, 1.3 miles away, in an attempt to dislodge Mullins. After he stopped, Richardson twice tried to pull Mullins out, before returning to the car and driving sharply and deliberately from side to side before mounting a grass verge, the court heard. Mullins was finally released but was then driven over again as Richardson reversed and drove away. A motorcyclist followed a trail of blood from the collision spot and discovered Mullins alone and barely breathing on the grass verge, the court heard. Emergency services attended but were unable to save Mullins, from Northwich, Cheshire, who died from multiple injuries. Richardson was arrested the next day after a police vehicle pursuit. He denied murder as he claimed he did not realise Mullins was underneath his car and said he did not get out of his vehicle to try to free him. In a statement, the family of Mullins said: “He was devoted to his family and our lives will never be the same. A gap has been left in our hearts and within his role as a headteacher of Stretford grammar school.” In his closing speech to jurors on Tuesday, Jaime Hamilton KC, defending, said: “You are likely to hold Simon Richardson in contempt. That contempt may well manifest itself in a loathing of Simon Richardson and, in fairness, you are probably right to. Because it is right that we acknowledge it was the actions of Simon Richardson that led to the death of Michael Mullins. “Not only is he responsible for the death of Michael Mullins, he acted in the most selfish of ways with one thought in his mind – himself. But that does not make him guilty of the homicide offences on this indictment.” Jurors went out to consider their verdict on Wednesday and returned to find Richardson guilty on Friday. The judge said she would sentence him on Monday. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jr.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, In future, German spies working for the BND foreign intelligence service will be able to conduct covert operations abroad By Bethany Bell Germany reporter Published 13 November 2026 Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers. But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara BÃ¼nger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police. The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution. In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained. For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it. In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage. This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons. Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified. That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved. Germany target of 'intensive' espionage, Merz says after suspected Russian spy arrest Published 22 October Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid Published 8 September Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack Published 2 September Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance. They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet. The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran. "We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers." In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty. German authorities say Russia was behind the attack. The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police. And Clara BÃ¼nger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monsterâ¦ summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of". The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and BÃ¼nger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era. "This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers." However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".
